qs.title: Stack DFS on Graph 1
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence of Graph 1 from vertex A, using a stack. Push neighbours in alphabetical order.

extra.unreached: G is never visited: its only edge is G → C, so G cannot be reached from A.
extra.answer: G is not reached. Its only edge is G → C, which leaves G, so no path from A leads to G.

qs.title: BFS on Graph 1
qs.problem: Find the BFS visit sequence of Graph 1 from vertex A, using a queue. Enqueue neighbours in alphabetical order.

extra.answer: G is unreached, as in Q1. Layers: 0: A · 1: B, C · 2: D, F · 3: E. Each vertex is visited at its fewest-edge distance from A.

qs.title: Topological order of Graph 1
qs.problem: Find a topological order of Graph 1 with the DFS-based (stack) algorithm from the slides. Push neighbours in alphabetical order and start the outer loop from A.

extra.answer: Another valid answer: recursive DFS with neighbours in alphabetical order gives G, A, C, B, F, D, E. Accept any order in which every edge points forward.

qs.title: Counting topological orders of Graph 2
qs.problem: How many distinct topological orders does Graph 2 have? Justify the count without listing blindly.

qs.title: Stack DFS on Graph 3
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence of Graph 3 from vertex A, using a stack. Push neighbours in reverse alphabetical order. Mark the pops that are discarded.

extra.answer: All 7 vertices are visited by the 7th pop, but the algorithm stops only when the stack is empty: 13 pops and 7 visits in total. In practice you may stop early once every vertex is visited.

qs.title: BFS on Graph 3
qs.problem: Find the BFS visit sequence of Graph 3 from vertex A, using a queue. Enqueue neighbours in reverse alphabetical order.

extra.answer: Compare with Q5: on the same graph, BFS spreads out layer by layer (D and B first), while DFS dives along A, B, C, D, …

qs.title: Topological order of Graph 3
qs.problem: Find a topological order of Graph 3 with the DFS-based (stack) algorithm. Push neighbours in reverse alphabetical order and start the outer loop from A. Bonus: is this the only valid order?

extra.answer: Bonus: this is the only valid order. Graph 3 contains the path A → B → C → D → E → F → G through all seven vertices. Each edge on it fixes the order of two consecutive vertices, so exactly one topological order exists.

qs.title: Stack DFS on Graph 4
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence of Graph 4 from vertex A, using a stack. Push neighbours in reverse alphabetical order. Ignore the edge weights.

extra.answer: Edge weights play no role in DFS.

qs.title: Uniform Cost Search on Graph 4
qs.problem: Use Uniform Cost Search (UCS) to find a lowest-cost path from A to G in Graph 4. Give every step.

qs.title: Topological order of Graph 4
qs.problem: Find a topological order of Graph 4 with the DFS-based (stack) algorithm. Push neighbours in alphabetical order and start the outer loop from A. Is this the only valid order?

extra.answer: Not unique. E is not ordered against C or D, so A, B, E, C, D, F, G is also valid. That is what recursive DFS with alphabetical neighbours produces.

qs.title: How many topological orders can a DAG have?
rules: construct a DAG for each count
qs.problem: For DAGs with N vertices, describe a graph whose number of valid topological orders is exactly N!, (N−1)!, …, 2!, 1.

qs.title: Stack DFS on the campus map
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence from A, using a stack. Push out-neighbours in alphabetical order.

extra.answer: When H is popped, its only out-neighbour C is already visited, so nothing is pushed. The loop C → F → H → C cannot trap DFS because a visited vertex is never expanded again.

qs.title: Same map, reverse push order
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence from A, using a stack. Push out-neighbours in reverse alphabetical order. Compare with Q1.

extra.answer: Only the push order changed from Q1, yet the visit sequence is completely different. Always check which neighbour ends up on top of the stack.

qs.title: BFS on the campus map
qs.problem: Find the BFS visit sequence from A, using a queue. Enqueue out-neighbours in alphabetical order. Compare with Q1.

extra.answer: BFS reaches vertices in order of the fewest edges from A: A · B, C · D, E, F · G, H. Compare with the DFS sequence in Q1 on the same graph.

qs.title: BFS starting inside the loop
qs.problem: Find the BFS visit sequence from C, using a queue. Enqueue out-neighbours in reverse alphabetical order.

extra.unreached: Some vertices are never visited: no path from the start reaches them.
extra.answer: C is visited when it is enqueued at the start, so the edge H → C never adds it again. A, B and D cannot be reached from C.

qs.title: Stack DFS on the server network
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence from A, using a stack. Push out-neighbours in reverse alphabetical order. Mark the pops that are discarded.

extra.unreached: Some vertices are never visited: no path from the start reaches them.
extra.answer: H is never visited: it has only outgoing edges, so nothing leads to it from A.

qs.title: DFS starting in the middle
qs.problem: Find the DFS visit sequence from D, using a stack. Push out-neighbours in alphabetical order.

extra.unreached: Some vertices are never visited: no path from the start reaches them.
extra.answer: A DFS from D only reaches what D can reach along the arrows. A, B, C and H stay unvisited; a single DFS does not restart elsewhere.

qs.title: BFS on the server network
qs.problem: Find the BFS visit sequence from A, using a queue. Enqueue out-neighbours in alphabetical order.

extra.unreached: Some vertices are never visited: no path from the start reaches them.
extra.answer: D is reached directly from A, so it is enqueued in the first layer even though B and C also point to it. H is unreachable.

qs.title: BFS from B, reverse order
qs.problem: Find the BFS visit sequence from B, using a queue. Enqueue out-neighbours in reverse alphabetical order.

extra.unreached: Some vertices are never visited: no path from the start reaches them.
extra.answer: Reverse order changes the sequence inside each layer (E before D), but the layers themselves stay the same: B · D, E · F, G.

qs.title: Course prerequisites
qs.problem: An arrow X → Y means course X must be taken before course Y. Find a topological order with the DFS finish-stack method. Push out-neighbours in alphabetical order and run the outer loop from A.

extra.answer: Many orders are valid here (42 in total). Any order in which every arrow points forward is correct.

qs.title: Build pipeline, labels out of order
qs.problem: Build steps are labelled A to G, but the labels do not follow the dependencies. Find a topological order with the DFS finish-stack method (push alphabetical, outer loop from A).

extra.answer: The outer loop starts from A, which depends on C and E. DFS still produces a valid order, because a vertex is only placed after everything it points to has finished.

qs.title: Is this schedule possible?
qs.problem: Find a topological order with the DFS finish-stack method, or show that none exists.

qs.title: Two separate projects
qs.problem: Two unrelated projects share one schedule. Find a topological order of all seven tasks with the DFS finish-stack method. Push out-neighbours in reverse alphabetical order.

extra.answer: The finish stack is kept across outer-loop restarts, so both projects end up in one order.

qs.title: Delivery routes
qs.problem: Use UCS to find the cheapest route from depot S to customer T. Give every step.

spec.answer: A and D both get cheaper after they are first enqueued (A: 4 → 3, D: 9 → 5). That is why a cost is only final when the vertex is dequeued.

extra.answer: A and D both get cheaper after they are first enqueued (A: 4 → 3, D: 9 → 5). That is why a cost is only final when the vertex is dequeued.

qs.title: Cheapest first step is a trap
qs.problem: Always taking the cheapest next edge would go S → A → C → T. Use UCS to find the lowest-cost path from S to T.

spec.answer: Greedy cheapest-edge gives S → A → C → T with cost 12. UCS compares total costs from S and finds a route costing 5.

extra.answer: Greedy cheapest-edge gives S → A → C → T with cost 12. UCS compares total costs from S and finds a route costing 5.

qs.title: Flights with a tie
qs.problem: Use UCS to find the cheapest itinerary from A to G. Watch what happens when two routes give the same cost.

spec.answer: Two routes to E cost 7 (A → C → E and A → C → B → E). The new cost is not strictly lower, so E keeps previous = C.

extra.answer: Two routes to E cost 7 (A → C → E and A → C → B → E). The new cost is not strictly lower, so E keeps previous = C.

qs.title: Flights from a different start
qs.problem: Same flight map as Q15, but start at B. Use UCS to find the cheapest path from B to G.

spec.answer: All costs are measured from the new start. Nothing carries over from Q15.

extra.answer: All costs are measured from the new start. Nothing carries over from Q15.

qs.title: Is there a route at all?
qs.problem: On the Q14 map, use UCS to find the cheapest path from C to D.

spec.answer: From C the only arrow goes to T, and T has no outgoing edges. The priority queue empties without dequeuing D, so there is no path.

extra.answer: From C the only arrow goes to T, and T has no outgoing edges. The priority queue empties without dequeuing D, so there is no path.
